milestone.title: Apple's '1984' commercial introduces Macintosh to a national audience
milestone.note: The Super Bowl broadcast made the graphical, mouse-driven Macintosh a mass-market cultural event and a landmark in computing and advertising history.

editorNote: Extra edition: one extraordinary minute of television turns a forthcoming personal computer into a national conversation.
morningLine: Macintosh steps from the trade press onto America’s biggest screen.

lead.headline: APPLE'S ‘1984’ SPOT PUTS MACINTOSH ON THE NATIONAL STAGE
lead.dek: A stark Super Bowl film promises a new kind of personal computer before viewers have even seen the machine itself.
body: During Super Bowl XVIII on January 22, Apple Computer used a single dramatic national broadcast to introduce the Macintosh as more than another machine. Ridley Scott’s film showed gray ranks of workers facing a giant screen until a lone runner smashed it, closing with Apple’s promise that 1984 would not resemble George Orwell’s 1984.

The commercial offered scarcely a conventional product demonstration. Its target was an idea: personal computing as an escape from conformity. That approach put the still-unreleased Macintosh before a mass audience with a cultural vocabulary far removed from memory counts and expansion slots.

Apple’s product plans supplied the substance behind the spectacle. Reports during the week described Macintosh as part of a broader 32-bit line alongside revised Lisa models, while Apple’s launch material emphasized a graphical display, mouse control, MacWrite and MacPaint at a suggested retail price of $2,495.

The advertisement’s reach made the Macintosh launch a public event before the January 24 unveiling. For the personal-computer business, the week marked a shift: machines would now be sold not only by specifications and price, but by an image of who their owners hoped to become.

stories.headline: APPLE READIES A 32-BIT FAMILY AROUND MACINTOSH AND LISA 2
body: Apple’s January plans linked the compact Macintosh to revised Lisa systems, placing the company’s graphical interface and mouse-driven approach across a broader product family.

MacWrite and MacPaint showed how fonts, cut-and-paste editing and bitmap drawing could make the interface tangible to ordinary users. The $2,495 suggested Macintosh price still put that experience well above bargain home computers.

stories.headline: COMMODORE 264 BETS ON SOFTWARE BUILT INTO THE MACHINE
body: At Winter CES, Commodore’s 264 and talking 364V prototypes pointed beyond the VIC-20 and Commodore 64. Their 3-PLUS-1 package placed word processing, files, spreadsheets and graphics in ROM.

The new family sacrificed direct Commodore 64 software compatibility, a consequential gamble when the C64 library was becoming one of the company’s strongest advantages. Pricing remained unsettled, leaving buyers to weigh convenience against continuity.

stories.headline: COLECO PROMISES A LARGER ADAM WORLD AMID QUALITY QUESTIONS
body: Coleco arrived at CES promising more peripherals and software for Adam, seeking to turn the all-in-one computer into an expanding home system.
But reports of defective early units continued to shadow the pitch. Dealers quoted roughly $700 to $799 in New York, making reliability as important as the machine’s ambitious bundle.
